descripcion_es: Common phrasal verbs grouped by topic: work, relationships, money and problems.
resumen: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle (up, out, off…) and change meaning. Learning them by topic helps you remember them and use them in conversation.

explicacion.texto: Some phrasal verbs are separable: the object can go in the middle or at the end (turn off the light / turn the light off), but if it is a pronoun it must go in the middle (turn it off). Others are never separated (look after the children, look after them).

filas: The company is taking on new staff.
to dismiss because there is not enough work (es: despedir)
to start, to found (es: montar, fundar)
She set up her own business.
to give to someone in authority (es: entregar)
Hand in your reports by Friday.
to have a good relationship (with) (es: llevarse bien con)
I get on well with my boss.
to argue and stop being friends (with) (es: enfadarse, reñir con)
She fell out with her sister.
to become friends again (es: hacer las paces)
They argued but made up the next day.
They broke up after five years.
My mother looks after my kids.
to raise a child (es: criar, educar)
She was brought up by her grandparents.
to keep money for something (es: ahorrar para)
I'm saving up for a car.
to have none left (es: quedarse sin)
to spend less (on) (es: recortar gastos en)
We need to cut back on spending.
to stop, to stop trying (es: dejar, rendirse)
to solve, to fix (es: resolver, arreglar)
to handle, to take action on (es: ocuparse de, afrontar)
My car broke down on the motorway.
They put off the meeting until Monday.
to discover, to learn (es: averiguar, enterarse)
He turned down the job offer.

items: With a pronoun, separable verbs always take it in the middle: put it off, not “put off it”.
Look after, deal with and get on with are inseparable.
Run out of and cut back on have two particles.

ejemplos.frase: My cousin set up a small bakery in her village.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi prima montó una pequeña panadería en su pueblo.

ejemplos.frase: We ran out of petrol in the middle of nowhere.
ejemplos.traduccion: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en mitad de la nada.

ejemplos.frase: They fell out over money, but they've made up now.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se enfadaron por dinero, pero ya han hecho las paces.

ejemplos.frase: The concert was called off because of the storm.
ejemplos.traduccion: El concierto se canceló por la tormenta.

ejemplos.frase: Could you look after my plants while I'm away?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Podrías cuidarme las plantas mientras estoy fuera?

ejemplos.frase: She turned down the offer because the salary was too low.
ejemplos.traduccion: Rechazó la oferta porque el sueldo era demasiado bajo.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The meeting is important, don't put off it.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The meeting is important, don't put it off.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a pronoun, a separable phrasal verb takes the pronoun in the middle.

errores_hispanohablantes.bien: We have run out of milk.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: To have none of something left is run out of.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Can you look my dog after?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Can you look after my dog?
They called off the trip. / They cancelled the trip.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: To cancel is cancel or call off; cancel out means to balance or neutralise an effect.

ejercicios.frase: Please fill ___ this form and sign it.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is fill in, “to complete a form”, from the table on work and paperwork. The clue is this form, a document that has to be completed. British English says fill in and American English fill out, so both in and out are accepted. It is separable: fill it in.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To complete a form is fill in (British) or fill out.
ejercicios.traduccion: Por favor, rellene este formulario y fírmelo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Fill up means to fill a container or a tank; it is not used with forms.
Fill on does not exist as a phrasal verb.

glosario.definicion_l: supply with information on a specific topic · represent the effect of shade or shadow on
write all the required information onto a form · make bigger or better or more complete
the phonological or orthographic sound or appearance of a word that can be used to describe or identify something · a category of things distinguished by some common characteristic or quality
used of the language of the deaf · a perceptible indication of something not immediately apparent (as a visible clue that something has happened)

ejercicios.frase: My grandmother looks ___ my children on Wednesdays.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is look after, “to take care of”, from the table on relationships and family. The clue is the grandmother and the children: the meaning is taking care of them. Look after is inseparable, as the rules and key points remind you: the object always goes after it, even if it is a pronoun (look after them).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To take care of is look after.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi abuela cuida de mis hijos los miércoles.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Look for means “to search for”; it would say the grandmother is searching for the children.
A word-for-word copy of Spanish “cuidar de”: the particle is after.
Look at means “to direct your eyes at”; it does not express taking care of.

glosario.definicion_l: keep under careful scrutiny
try to locate or discover, or try to establish the existence of · be excited or anxious about

ejercicios.frase: Lend me twenty euros and I'll pay you ___ next week.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is pay back, “to return money”, from the money table. The clue is lend me twenty euros: what is lent is paid back. It is separable, and here the object is the person (you), which goes in the middle: pay you back.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To return money is pay back.
ejercicios.traduccion: Préstame veinte euros y te los devuelvo la semana que viene.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Pay off means to settle a debt completely or to bring good results; to return money to someone, use pay back.
A word-for-word copy of Spanish “te lo vuelvo a pagar”: to return money is pay back.

glosario.definicion_l: act or give recompense in recognition of someone's behavior or actions · take vengeance on or get even
bestow a quality on · give temporarily; let have for a limited time

ejercicios.frase: After ten years together, they broke ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is break up, “to end a relationship”, from the relationships table. The clue is after ten years together: it is about the end of a couple. Break up has no object in this sentence; if the other person is mentioned, add with (She broke up with him).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To end a relationship is break up.
ejercicios.traduccion: Después de diez años juntos, rompieron.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Break down means to stop working (a machine) or to lose control emotionally; it does not mean ending a relationship.
Break out means to start suddenly (a war, a fire) or to escape; it does not refer to a couple.

glosario.definicion_l: to cause to separate and go in different directions · discontinue an association or relation; go different ways
make ineffective · make a mathematical, chemical, or grammatical analysis of; break down into components or essential features

ejercicios.frase: The company had to lay ___ fifty employees.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is lay off, “to dismiss because there is not enough work”, from the work table. The clue is the company and fifty employees: a reduction in staff. Lay off is different from fire or sack, which mean dismissing because of the worker's fault; lay off is due to the company's economic reasons.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To dismiss because there is not enough work is lay off.
ejercicios.traduccion: La empresa tuvo que despedir a cincuenta empleados.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Lay out means “to arrange, to spread out” or “to present”; it does not mean dismissing.
Lay down means “to put on the ground” or “to establish” rules; it does not mean dismissing.
Influenced by the opposite, take on (to employ); to dismiss is lay off.

glosario.significado: despedir (por falta de trabajo o por motivos económicos)
glosario.definicion_l: put an end to a state or an activity · dismiss, usually for economic reasons
a worker who is hired to perform a job

ejercicios.frase: The match was ___ because of the snow.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is call off, “to cancel”, from the table on money and problems. The clue is because of the snow: the match does not take place. Here it appears in the passive (was called off), very common in sports news. It is equivalent to the Latin-based verb cancel.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To cancel an event is call off.
ejercicios.traduccion: El partido se suspendió por la nieve.

por_opcion.called off: Correct: call off means “to cancel, to suspend” an event.
por_opcion.turned down: Incorrect: turn down means “to refuse” an offer or an invitation, or to lower the volume; it is not used with a match.
por_opcion.set up: Incorrect: set up means “to start, to found” (set up a business); it makes no sense with the snow.

glosario.definicion_l: postpone indefinitely or annul something that was scheduled · give the calls (to the dancers) for a square dance
lighter consisting of a thin piece of wood or cardboard tipped with combustible chemical; ignites with friction · a formal contest in which two or more persons or teams compete

ejercicios.frase: I can't ___ my landlord; he's very unfriendly.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is get on with, “to have a good relationship with”, from the relationships table. The clue is he's very unfriendly, which explains why the relationship is bad, and the object my landlord, which requires with. Get on with has two particles and is never separated.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To have a good relationship with someone is get on with.
ejercicios.traduccion: No consigo llevarme bien con mi casero; es muy antipático.

por_opcion.get on with: Correct: to have a good relationship with someone.
por_opcion.fall out: Incorrect: fall out means “to argue and stop being friends” and would need with before the person (fall out with); also, it makes no sense with can't.
por_opcion.make up: Incorrect: make up means “to become friends again” (after an argument) and does not take the person as a direct object; you would say make up with.

glosario.definicion_l: have smooth relations
a landowner who leases to others
not easy to understand or use · not disposed to friendship or friendliness

ejercicios.frase: Prices are rising, so we have to ___ on eating out.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is cut back on, “to spend less on”, from the money table. The clue is prices are rising and the preposition on, already written after the gap. It is a two-particle phrasal verb: cut back + on + the thing you spend less on. Eating out means “eating away from home”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To spend less on something is cut back on.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los precios están subiendo, así que tenemos que recortar en comer fuera.

por_opcion.cut back: Correct: with on it forms cut back on, “to spend less on”.
por_opcion.give up: Incorrect: give up means “to stop” a habit completely and is not used with on.
por_opcion.pay back: Incorrect: pay back means “to return money” and is not used with on.

glosario.definicion_l: eat at a restaurant or at somebody else's home
a growth in strength or number or importance · the act of changing location in an upward direction

ejercicios.frase: Don't worry, the technician will ___ the problem.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is sort out, “to solve, to fix”, from the problems table. The clue is the technician and the problem: a technician solves problems. Sort out is separable (sort it out) and very common in informal British English.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To solve a problem is sort out.
ejercicios.traduccion: No te preocupes, el técnico resolverá el problema.

por_opcion.find out: Incorrect: find out means “to discover”; you discover the cause, you don't solve the problem.
por_opcion.break down: Incorrect: break down means “to stop working” and takes no object; it would say the technician stops working.

glosario.definicion_l: arrange or order by classes or categories · make free from confusion or ambiguity; make clear
someone whose occupation involves training in a specific technical process · someone known for high skill in some intellectual or artistic technique

ejercicios.frase: The exam is on Monday. You can't put off it.
respuestas: The exam is on Monday. You can't put it off.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is put off, “to postpone”, which is separable. The rule from the rules and key points applies: with a pronoun, a separable verb takes the pronoun in the middle. The clue is it, which replaces the exam. So: put it off.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With a pronoun, a separable phrasal verb takes the pronoun in the middle.
ejercicios.traduccion: El examen es el lunes. No puedes aplazarlo.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The exam is on Monday. You can't put off it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence without correcting it: the pronoun goes between put and off.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The exam is on Monday. You can't put it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without off it means “to put it somewhere”; the particle is essential.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The exam is on Monday. You can't it put off.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The object pronoun does not go before the verb as in Spanish.

glosario.definicion_l: hold back to a later time · cause to feel intense dislike or distaste

ejercicios.frase: We've run out bread. Can you buy some?
respuestas: We've run out of bread. Can you buy some?
We have run out of bread. Can you buy some?
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is run out of, “to have none left”, from the money table. The clue is Can you buy some?, which shows there is no bread left. Run out of has two particles, and the sentence forgot of, which introduces what has been used up.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To have none of something left is run out of.
ejercicios.traduccion: Nos hemos quedado sin pan. ¿Puedes comprar?

errores_previstos.respuesta: We've run out bread. Can you buy some?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence without correcting it: of is missing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We've run out from bread. Can you buy some?
errores_previstos.explicacion: The correct particle is of, not from.

errores_previstos.respuesta: We've run off bread. Can you buy some?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Run off means “to leave quickly, running”; to have none left is run out of.

ejercicios.frase: I was brought out in a small village in Asturias.
respuestas: I was brought up in a small village in Asturias.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is bring up, “to raise a child”, from the table on relationships and family. The clue is in a small village: it is about where someone was raised. It is often used in the passive (be brought up) when the subject is the person who was raised. The correct particle is up, not out.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To be raised as a child is be brought up.
ejercicios.traduccion: Me crie en un pueblo pequeño de Asturias.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I was brought out in a small village in Asturias.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence without correcting it: to be raised is be brought up.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I was grown up in a small village in Asturias.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Grow up has no passive; you would say I grew up in a small village.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I was bring up in a small village in Asturias.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After was you need the past participle brought.

glosario.definicion_l: summon into action or bring into existence, often as if by magic · look after a child until it is an adult
make manifest · bring out of a specific state
a mainly residential district of Manhattan; ‘the Village’ became a home for many writers and artists in the 20th century · a community of people smaller than a town

ejercicios.enunciado: Replace the offer with the pronoun it.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is turn down, “to refuse”, from the problems table. The rule for separable verbs applies: with a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle. The clue is the instruction, which asks you to replace the offer with it. So: turned it down.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With a pronoun, this separable phrasal verb takes it in the middle.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With a separable verb, the pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.
Without down it means “turned it round”; the particle is essential.

glosario.significado: rechazar (una oferta, una invitación); también bajar el volumen
glosario.definicion_l: not accept as true · refuse entrance or membership
the verbal act of offering · something offered (as a proposal or bid)

respuestas: She set up her own business
She set her own business up
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is set up, “to start, to found”, from the work table. It is separable: with a noun, the object can go after the particle or between the verb and the particle, so both orders are accepted. With a long object such as her own business, it is more natural to put it at the end.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Set up means to start or found.

errores_previstos.respuesta: she set her up own business
errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle cannot go inside the noun phrase her own business.

errores_previstos.respuesta: she up set her own business
errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle goes after the verb.

glosario.definicion_l: set up or found · create by putting components or members together
a commercial or industrial enterprise and the people who constitute it · the activity of providing goods and services involving financial and commercial and industrial aspects

ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is find out, “to discover, to learn”, from the problems table. It is separable: with the noun the truth, the object can go after the particle or in the middle, so both orders are accepted. The past of find is irregular: found.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle goes after the verb.
The particle cannot separate the article from its noun.

glosario.definicion_l: establish after a calculation, investigation, experiment, survey, or study · get to know or become aware of, usually accidentally
United States abolitionist and feminist who was freed from slavery and became a leading advocate of the abolition of slavery and for the rights of women… · a fact that has been verified

ejercicios.frase: I'm saving ___ for a new laptop.
ejercicios.explicacion: The phrasal verb practised is save up (for), “to keep money (for)”, from the money table. The clue is for a new laptop, the goal of the saving. Save up stresses that money is built up little by little for a purpose; save on its own also exists, but here the particle up is required.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To keep money for something is save up for.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estoy ahorrando para un portátil nuevo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Save out does not exist as a phrasal verb; to keep money for something is save up for.
Save on means “to spend less on” something (save on electricity), not to keep money for something.

glosario.definicion_l: a portable computer small enough to use in your lap

descripcion_larga_es: This card brings together everyday phrasal verbs grouped by topic: work (take on, lay off, set up, hand in), relationships (get on with, fall out, make up, break up, bring up) and money and problems (pay back, save up, cut back on, sort out, call off, put off). Learning them by field makes them easier to remember and use in conversation. Spanish speakers find them hard because the particle changes the meaning completely and cannot be worked out from Spanish.

contexto.que_es: It is a set of high-frequency phrasal verbs organised by topic. Each one has its own meaning, which must be learnt like a new word, and a specific syntax: separable, inseparable or with two particles.
contexto.por_que_importa: In everyday conversation and at work, native speakers use phrasal verbs all the time (They laid off 200 workers, The match was called off), and anyone who doesn't know them misses a lot of information. Getting the particle wrong changes the meaning (break up is ending a relationship; break down, to stop working), and putting the pronoun in the wrong place sounds clearly incorrect.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In informal and neutral registers: talking about work, family, a partner, money, or plans that are postponed or cancelled. In formal texts the Latin-based verb is usually preferred (cancel, postpone, recruit, dismiss). Spanish speakers tend to use only those Latin-based verbs, which sounds stiff in conversation.
